title: What does a Washington accident prevention program require for safety orientation and training?
description: WAC 296-800-140: the written accident prevention program, seven safety orientation elements, pre-assignment training and committees, as at November 2026.
shortAnswer: Washington's core safety rule, WAC 296-800-140, requires every employer covered by it to establish, supervise and enforce a written accident prevention program that is effective in practice. The program must include a safety orientation with seven listed elements, a safety committee or safety meetings, and training programs that give employees on-the-job instruction about hazards before their job assignment. The Washington State Department of Labor and Industries enforces the rule.
keyTakeaways: WAC 296-800-14005 requires a formal, written accident prevention program tailored to the workplace and its hazards, by whatever name the employer uses.
The safety orientation must cover seven elements, from the overall safety program to identifying hazardous chemicals and what to do after accidental exposure.
WAC 296-800-14020 requires on-the-job instruction before job assignment on hazards such as powered materials handling equipment, machine tools, toxic materials and utility systems.
Employers with 11 or more employees on the same shift at the same location must run a safety committee; smaller workplaces may hold monthly safety meetings instead.
The test throughout is that the program is "effective in practice": a written plan that is not followed or taught does not comply.
regulator: Washington State Department of Labor and Industries (L&I)
appliesTo: Employers covered by chapter 296-800 WAC, the core safety and health rules adopted under chapter 49.17 RCW
All employees, who must receive a safety orientation and pre-assignment hazard instruction
Employers with 11 or more employees on the same shift at the same location (safety committee); smaller or dispersed workforces (safety meetings option)

sections.heading: What is Washington's accident prevention program rule?

blocks.text: It is the general safety program requirement in Washington's core rules. WAC 296-800-140 states: "You must establish, supervise and enforce an accident prevention program (APP) that is effective in practice. (You may call this your total safety and health plan.)" The rule is adopted under chapter 49.17 RCW, the Washington Industrial Safety and Health Act, and enforced by the Department of Labor and Industries.

The section points to three subsections: WAC 296-800-14005 (develop a formal, written program), WAC 296-800-14020 (develop, supervise, implement and enforce training programs that are effective in practice) and WAC 296-800-14025 (make sure the program is effective in practice). The rule took effect on September 1, 2001, and was last amended by WSR 18-22-116, effective December 7, 2018. This page states the position as at November 2026.

Washington's approach is similar in purpose to California's Injury and Illness Prevention Program and Minnesota's AWAIR program, but the detail differs. Compare [Cal/OSHA IIPP training requirements](/regulations/cal-osha-iipp-training-requirements) and [Minnesota AWAIR](/regulations/minnesota-awair-safety-program-training).

sections.heading: What must the written program contain?

blocks.text: The program must be outlined in writing and "tailored to the needs of your particular workplace or operation and to the types of hazards involved." WAC 296-800-14005 explains that the term refers to the written plan to prevent accidents, illnesses and injuries, which "may be known as your safety and health plan, injury prevention program, or by some other name."

At a minimum, the program must contain two elements: a safety orientation, described below, and a safety and health committee under WAC 296-800-130. The training programs required by WAC 296-800-14020 sit alongside these. A generic template that does not reflect the employer's own hazards would fail the tailoring requirement even if it lists every heading.

L&I publishes accident prevention program templates for general industry and for construction, and its [Safety & Health page](https://lni.wa.gov/safety-health/) noted in November 2026 that both templates had been updated. A template is a starting point; the orientation and hazard sections still need to be completed for the actual workplace.

sections.heading: What must a Washington safety orientation cover?

blocks.text: The safety orientation must cover seven elements listed in WAC 296-800-14005(2)(a). They combine general content about the program with job-specific instruction for the employee's first assignment.

blocks.text: Elements (ii), (v) and (vii) cannot be delivered generically, because they depend on the job, the PPE issued and the chemicals present. A short office module plus a supervisor-led checklist at the work area is a common way to cover both halves. See [how to structure onboarding for regulated roles](/guides/how-to-structure-onboarding-for-regulated-roles).

sections.heading: What training programs does WAC 296-800-14020 require?

blocks.text: Employers must run training programs "to improve the skill, awareness, and competency of all your employees in the field of occupational safety and health," including on-the-job instruction before job assignment. The rule names four example hazard areas for pre-assignment instruction: safe use of powered materials-handling equipment such as forklifts and backhoes; safe use of machine tool operations; use of toxic materials; and operation of utility systems.

The list says "such as," so it is not exhaustive. Any hazard in the employee's assignment that needs instruction to work safely falls under the duty. Specific Washington rules for forklifts, lockout, respiratory protection and other hazards have their own training provisions, and the APP training program is the frame that ties them to each role. A [training matrix](/guides/how-to-build-a-training-matrix) listing roles against hazards makes the pre-assignment duty checkable.

sections.heading: When is a safety committee required instead of safety meetings?

blocks.text: A safety committee is required when an employer has 11 or more employees on the same shift at the same location. Employers with 10 or fewer employees, or with larger workforces split into shifts or widely separate locations of 10 or fewer, may hold safety meetings instead.

blocks.text: Because both forums must evaluate accident investigations and the program itself, they are a practical place to decide when retraining is needed after an incident and to record that decision.

sections.heading: What does "effective in practice" mean for training evidence?

blocks.text: It means compliance is judged by what happens at the work area, not only by the document. WAC 296-800-14025 requires the employer to "establish, supervise, and enforce your accident prevention program in a manner that is effective in practice," and the training subsection uses the same phrase. Attendance alone may not show that employees can apply what they were taught.

Useful evidence includes orientation checklists signed by both the employee and the supervisor, observed demonstrations for equipment and PPE, and committee minutes showing that investigation findings led to training changes. See [how to evidence training effectiveness to a regulator](/guides/how-to-evidence-training-effectiveness-to-a-regulator).

blocks.title: Health care settings
blocks.text: Hospitals, home health, hospice and home care agencies, behavioral health programs and certain other health care settings also have a separate workplace violence prevention plan and training duty under chapter 49.19 RCW. See [Washington health care workplace violence training](/regulations/washington-healthcare-workplace-violence-training).

sections.heading: How does Knowledge Foundry approach this?

blocks.text: Knowledge Foundry represents the seven orientation elements and the pre-assignment hazards as separate requirements linked to each role, so an orientation record shows which element was covered, by whom and against which program version. See [operational procedures programs](/programs/operational-procedures).

faqs.q: Does a small Washington employer need a written accident prevention program?
faqs.a: WAC 296-800-14005 requires a formal program outlined in writing, tailored to the workplace and its hazards, with no small employer exemption stated in that subsection. Small employers can choose monthly safety meetings instead of a safety committee if they meet the conditions in WAC 296-800-13025.

faqs.q: Is annual safety training required under WAC 296-800-140?
faqs.a: The APP rule does not set an annual interval. It requires a safety orientation, on-the-job instruction before job assignment, and training programs that are effective in practice. Specific hazard rules may set their own refresher intervals.

faqs.q: How long must safety committee minutes be kept in Washington?
faqs.a: WAC 296-800-13020 requires minutes from each safety committee meeting to be preserved for one year and made available for review by Department of Labor and Industries safety and health consultation personnel. Safety meetings need only a record of attendance and topics.

faqs.q: Can the accident prevention program have a different name?
faqs.a: Yes. WAC 296-800-14005 says the program may be known as a safety and health plan, injury prevention program, or by some other name, and WAC 296-800-140 allows it to be called a total safety and health plan.
